<description>
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process.
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention.
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.
</description>

[2026-11-16] rc:4589102884 inline on src/wallet/wallet.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-16):

In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (77e82fcc3d5baaadd5512ba58b3f677e5498ed17)

[quoted text omitted]
This still applies to the latest push. Here is the suggestion updated with the new behavior when the move fails:

```
Currently, MigrateToSQLite loads all BDB records into memory, deletes the original database, creates the sqlite database in its place and writes the records to it. If anything fails after the delete, the wallet is left partly in sqlite format with legacy records, and the user has to restore the backup manually.

Instead, build the sqlite database in a temporary directory next to the original database file, and once all records are written, rename it into place. For wallet directories the rename replaces the original wallet.dat atomically, so a failure at any earlier point leaves the original untouched. A wallet that is a plain file becomes a wallet directory, which cannot replace the file atomically, so the original file is erased just before the move. Failures from that point on throw, so the caller restores the backup.

Before the move, remove any leftover journal at the destination, since SQLite would roll it back into the new database when it is opened and corrupt it.
```

In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (77e82fcc3d5baaadd5512ba58b3f677e5498ed17)

Thanks, latest update covers all three concerns, even though it uses directory iteration instead of `CWallet:::Erase`, so carries some of the risk of the banned `fs::remove_all`. But deleting whatever is in the temporary directory is simpler than removing the files by name, and the check that the directory didn't exist before makes it safer.

One thing I got wrong in [my suggestion above](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4553153518) is the final check. Checking whether the directory still exists after removing it is unnecessary and slightly worse than checking the error from `fs::remove`. If any file is left inside, removing the directory fails with "Directory not empty", so its error already reports every way the cleanup can fail. If the directory was never created, `fs::remove` returns false with no error. Meanwhile `fs::exists(fs::symlink_status(...))` returns false when `lstat` fails for another reason (like permission denied), so it can report a successful cleanup when it couldn't tell. This would be simpler:

```cpp
fs::remove(tmp_wallet_path, ec);
if (ec) {
    error += Untranslated(" ") + strprintf(_("The temporary database at %s could not be removed."), fs::PathToString(tmp_wallet_path));
}
```

In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (77e82fcc3d5baaadd5512ba58b3f677e5498ed17)

Thanks, the reworded comment makes it clear these files weren't created by this code.

I'd still lean toward the simpler alternative from my comment above, though: return an error for any file found here instead of checking whether it looks like a database and deleting it otherwise. It's less code, it never deletes a file this code didn't create, and since failures here now restore the backup, a user who hits it gets an error naming the file and can move it out of the way and try again. Something like:

```cpp
// Other files of this db should never be present at the destination, but an interrupted earlier migration or an
// outside process may leave them there. A leftover journal, for example, would be rolled back into the moved db
// by SQLite, corrupting it. Return an error rather than guessing whether a file is safe to delete.
std::error_code ec;
for (const fs::path& file : files) {
    const fs::path leftover{dst_path / fs::path{file.filename()}};
    if (leftover == dst_file) continue; // Replaced atomically by the rename below
    if (fs::symlink_status(leftover, ec).type() != fs::file_type::not_found) {
        return util::Error{strprintf(_("Error: Unable to move the wallet db, unexpected file %s found at the destination. Move it elsewhere and try again."), fs::PathToString(leftover))};
    }
}
```

Current approach is fine too if you prefer it.

[2026-11-16] rc:4589667685 inline on src/wallet/wallet.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-16):
In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (77e82fcc3d5baaadd5512ba58b3f677e5498ed17)

Since `MigrateLegacyToDescriptor` restores the backup only when `MigrateToSQLite` throws, it would be good if the comment here warned more directly that nothing after this point may return false. Something like:

```cpp
// From here on, the original db may have been erased or replaced. Never return false after this point: the caller
// treats false as "the original db is unchanged" and skips restoring the backup. Throw instead, so the caller
// deletes the wallet files and restores the backup.
```

Might also suggest a comment and assert clarifying why the Erase() call is safe:

```cpp
// A plain wallet file (its db file is the wallet path itself) becomes a wallet directory. As a file cannot be
// atomically replaced by a directory, the original db is erased first in that case. The original db is a single
// file, so if Erase() fails nothing was removed, and returning false is still correct.
if (db_file == dst_wallet_dir) {
    Assert(m_database->Files().size() == 1);
    if (auto res{m_database->Erase()}; !res) return remove_tmp_and_fail(util::ErrorString(res));
}
```

Returning false after the `Erase()` fails is only right because the legacy database is a single file. If `Erase()` could remove some files and then fail, the backup wouldn't be restored. Throwing wouldn't help in that case either: the rollback removes the same files with the throwing `fs::remove`, which would probably fail again, outside the try block. So it seems best to document the assumption, and the assert would catch it if `Files()` ever returned more than one file here.
[2026-11-16] rc:4589667952 inline on src/wallet/wallet.h by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-16):

Thanks for documenting this. Besides [a clearer warning in `MigrateToSQLite`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4589667685), since a stray `return false` after the original is replaced would silently skip the restore, it might be worth making the contract part of the return type, for example:

```cpp
enum class MigrateDbResult {
    SUCCESS,          //!< The wallet now uses the new SQLite database
    FAILED_UNCHANGED, //!< The new database couldn't be built and the original is untouched, so no restore is needed
};
```

Then `return false` doesn't compile, and each early return has to say that the original is unchanged, which makes a mistake after the point of no return easier to spot in review. Not needed for this PR though.
